Hello, I’m GPTREI, your requirements elicitation assistant. I’ll be gathering detailed information about the WARC Tools Phase III project to make sure we capture the full scope and requirements clearly.

Before we begin, are you aligned with this interview’s scope, or do you expect it to cover something different?

Yes, I’m aligned with that scope. We’re focused on expanding the WARC Tools suite for large-scale web archive management, especially migration, repackaging, inspection, reporting, duplicate detection, and validation after conversion. I’d expect the discussion to stay around operational needs for archivists and engineers, plus deployment and scaling across institutions.
Thank you. To start off, could you please introduce yourself and your connection to this project?

I’m speaking as someone on the institutional side who works with web archive operations and the people who manage these collections. I’m familiar with the day-to-day needs around processing archived web content, checking results, and making sure the tools fit into shared workflows across teams and institutions.
Thank you. Could you describe the current process or system you use today for migrating, repackaging, inspecting, reporting on, deduplicating, and validating archived web content?

Right now, it’s a mix of separate tools and a fair amount of manual coordination. People typically run conversions or checks in batches, then inspect outputs and compare reports by hand or with scripts, which works but gets cumbersome once the collections get large. Validation and duplicate checking are especially important, but they’re not always part of one smooth workflow today.
What current processes do you want to improve or change, or what features are you hoping to get from this project?

We want a more integrated workflow so staff can move from migration to validation without stitching together so many separate steps. It would help a lot to have better batch processing, clearer reporting, and easier ways to inspect records when something looks wrong. We’re also hoping for stronger duplicate detection and more confidence that content and metadata survive the conversion correctly.

So the main features you want are an integrated migration-to-validation workflow, better batch processing, clearer reporting, easier record inspection, stronger duplicate detection, and content/metadata verification after conversion, right?
Yes, that’s right. The main goal is to make the whole process more reliable and less manual, especially when we’re working with large collections and multiple institutions.
Are there any other features you would like to see in this project, perhaps something that has not been the primary focus so far?

I’d also expect good support for collaborative deployment and testing, since different institutions may want to try the tools in their own environment before rolling them out more broadly. It would be useful if the tools were easy to configure and if we could get logs or output that help troubleshoot problems without digging too deeply into the internals. I’m not sure yet whether there are other major features beyond that.
Based on your description, do you think role-based access or permission controls should also be included for collaborative use across institutions?

Yes, I think some form of role-based access would make sense, especially if multiple people are using the same deployment or shared test environment. At minimum, we’d want to separate who can run jobs, who can review results, and who can change configurations. I’d need to check whether we need finer-grained permissions across institutions, but the basic control model seems important.

Considering the features we’ve identified so far—integrated migration and validation workflow, batch processing, reporting, record inspection, duplicate detection, content/metadata verification, collaborative deployment and testing, configurable setup, troubleshooting logs, and role-based access—how would you prioritize these?

I’d put integrated migration and validation first, because that’s the core workflow we need to trust. After that, batch processing and content or metadata verification are probably the next most important, since scale and correctness are the main pain points. Reporting, record inspection, duplicate detection, and troubleshooting logs would follow closely, and collaborative deployment with role-based access is important too, but more as an enabling layer for shared use.
Please elaborate on what you want the integrated migration and validation workflow to accomplish, step by step, from the moment a job is prepared until the results are accepted.

First, someone should be able to define the source collection, the target format, and any relevant settings in one place. Then the system should run the migration, automatically validate the output for basic structural and metadata checks, and flag any records that need attention. After that, a reviewer should be able to inspect the flagged items, look at a report of what changed or failed, and either accept the run or send it back for correction.

It seems like you need a single place to define the source collection, target format, and settings, then run migration, automatic validation, flagging of issues, reviewer inspection, reporting of changes/failures, and acceptance or correction of the run. Can you describe more about what “basic structural and metadata checks” should include?

At a minimum, we’d want to confirm that the WARC files are readable, that the records are packaged correctly, and that the expected headers and metadata fields are present. We’d also want to check that the conversion didn’t lose obvious information like URLs, timestamps, or content types, and that the record counts line up with what we expected from the source. If there are any checks beyond that, I’d need to verify with the team.
Are there any current systems or tools you already use today for these structural, metadata, or record-count checks?

Yes, in some cases we use existing archive validation scripts and a few ad hoc checks people run during QA, but they’re not always consistent across teams. For record counts and metadata review, a lot of it still ends up being manual or spread across different tools. I don’t know of one single system that covers all of it well today.
Which of the requirements we’ve discussed would you say is most critical for the first release, and which could wait for a later phase?

For the first release, I’d say integrated migration with automatic validation is the most critical, along with the basic reporting needed to judge whether a run passed or failed. Batch processing is also important if we want it to handle real collections at scale. Features like more advanced record inspection, duplicate detection, and richer collaborative controls could probably wait for a later phase.
Who else do you think has valuable insights into the project, and whose needs need to be considered, and why?

Archivists are key because they understand the collection workflows and what counts as acceptable preservation quality. Engineers and operations staff matter too since they’ll be the ones deploying, running, and troubleshooting the tools at scale. I’d also include QA or validation staff, because they tend to catch the practical edge cases that make or break whether a migration is trusted.
What would you consider a successful deployment of WARC Tools Phase III?

A successful deployment would be one where teams can confidently migrate ARC to WARC at scale, verify the results without a lot of manual work, and trust the reports enough to use them in real production decisions. It also needs to be stable enough that multiple institutions can set it up, test it, and operate it with minimal support. If people can use it to process large batches and know when something needs attention, that would feel like success to us.

To summarize, we discussed an integrated migration-and-validation workflow, basic structural and metadata checks, batch processing, reporting, record inspection, duplicate detection, troubleshooting logs, collaborative deployment, and role-based access, with first-release priority on integrated migration, automatic validation, basic reporting, and batch processing. Is there anything else you would like to add?

One thing I’d add is that we need the workflow to be reproducible, so if someone reruns the same job with the same inputs, they should get comparable results and be able to audit what changed. It would also help to have clear exportable logs or artifacts for sharing between institutions when something fails or needs review. Beyond that, I think the summary is pretty close to what we need.
